en.title: Buses and trains
en.summary: Public transport: asking about services, platforms and changes, and understanding announcements.

paragraphs: Buses and trains are the main way of travelling in many English-speaking cities. In this lesson you will ask about times and platforms, understand announcements and talk about delays.
A traveller is at Birmingham New Street station, planning a journey to Leeds.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Excuse me, which platform does the train to Leeds leave from?

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.text: Platform four. It leaves at ten past nine.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Do I need to change anywhere?

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.text: No, it is a direct train. It arrives in Leeds at ten forty.

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.text: At the moment, yes, but I would listen for announcements. There are sometimes delays on this line.

lines.speaker: Announcement
lines.text: The nine-ten service to Leeds is delayed by about fifteen minutes. We apologise for the inconvenience.

lines.speaker: Traveller
lines.text: Thank you. I will wait on the platform.

paragraphs: **1. The present simple gives timetables.** Even for future events, a scheduled departure or arrival uses the present simple. See Introduction to Grammar: Future and other tenses.

blocks.html:
EventExample
departureThe train leaves at 9:10.
arrivalIt arrives in Leeds at 10:40.
questionWhat time does the bus leave?
negativeThe bus doesn't stop here.

paragraphs: **2. Need to, have to and must express obligation.** Need to and have to describe what the situation requires; must is stronger and more personal. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

blocks.html:
PhraseExample
need toDo I need to change?
have toYou have to validate your ticket.
mustYou must not smoke on the platform.
don't have toYou don't have to book a seat.

items: A platform is where you wait for and board a train.
Single or one-way means a journey in one direction; return or round trip means there and back.
Delayed means later than planned; cancelled means it will not run.
On time, late and early are the common words for punctuality.

paragraphs: On many British trains you must keep your ticket until you leave the station, because inspectors may check it. Announcements are made in a formal, polite style, often beginning with the words Ladies and gentlemen or We apologise for.
